body: Contrasts were everywhere in the eighties. The decade would see us going from mainframes to PCs, computer art at its peak to it’s death, communities formed yet artists were more disparate than ever, we went from fearing machines to…fearing them slightly less. But millions—vastly more than possible before—were growing to love them.

Humanity’s relationship with machines transformed over the course of the decade, as mass media entered homes with PCs, VHS and video games. While derided by some at the time as toys, these early mass media devices propelled entire genres, including computer, digital and video art. The early practitioners saw something that few others did. By calling them toys, critics at the time were infantilizing their use but really they were unable to glimpse the same—more accurate—future as the pioneers of this decade. Le Random was fortunate enough to speak to many of them.

For more context, we suggest watching or listening (transcript) to our Ch 6 Artist Discussion with Mark Wilson⁠, ⁠Copper Giloth⁠, ⁠Dan Sandin⁠, ⁠David Em⁠, ⁠William Latham⁠, ⁠Stephen Todd⁠, ⁠Darcy Gerbarg⁠ + ⁠Geoff Davis⁠⁠⁠.
Additionally, in this piece on Le Random Editorials, Operator speaks with Rebecca Allen, one of the most significant voices from the decade.

Community formation was also an important aspect of the decade. Curated by Darcy Gerbarg and later Copper Giloth, the annual SIGGRAPH computer art show became instrumental in establishing a community of artists in the decade. The shows demonstrated the importance of in-person events for digital communities. The formation of the demoscene in Europe was another important community of the decade.

Finally, software and network advancements also reshaped the decade, as HyperCard and Director transformed multimedia, while Tim Berners-Lee had a radically impactful technological invention in store for us at the end of the decade with the World Wide Web.

body: Vera Molnár was heavily involved with Sorbonne University throughout the 1980s. In 1980, she and Franćois established the Centre de Recherche Expérimentale et Informatique des Arts Visuels (CREIAV). From 1985 to 1990, she taught fine art, aesthetics and art history at the Sorbonne’s Department of Plastic Arts and Art Sciences. This period was also fruitful for her practice, as it included some of her most well-known projects, such as Lettres à ma mère (1981-1990). Molnár stopped using plotters in 1991 and switched to prints. 1980 was a big year for Vera, as it also marked the publishing of her first artist’s book Un pourcent de désordre (One per cent disorder) by Wedgepress & Cheese in Bjärred (Sweden).

body: This early computer graphics art video by Dan Sandin, Tom DeFanti and Mimi Shevitz uses the image processor as a musical instrument, generating variations on a spiral motif synchronized with an eclectic audio track. Created in 1980 and 1981 by combining Tom DeFanti’s GRASS system and the Sandin Image Processor, this innovative piece was among the first video art works included in the Museum of Modern Art’s collection. The work thus stands as an important achievement in not only early computer animation but in digital art and more broadly the intersection of technology and visual art.

body: A representational beginning to the decade, which would be responsible for the explosion of “digital art” due to the emerging prevalence of computers and digital devices becoming smaller and entering homes. Besides the micro effect on artists, on a macro level, the impact of these devices cannot be overstated. Devices such as the VHS machine, the Apple II and the Atari 2600 would revolutionize the personal relationship between humanity and digital devices. Wilson, a pioneer of digital art, began his career as a traditionally trained artist. In 1980, he purchased a microcomputer, taught himself programming and started producing plotter drawings. His work today is featured in the collection at the V&A. This marks an important example in the development of generative art that would symbolize the 1980s: the increased accessibility of computers.

Divisibility I is a series that Mohr began in 1980 and would last until 1984. Again, Mohr returns to the cube as his main point of departure and inspiration. The series consists of various cubes that have been divided, cut and rearranged.

body: This exhibit stands out as a key moment in the transition from video art to video game art. Copper Giloth bridged the gap between the rapidly rising popularity of video games and video art. Her piece, From Video Games to Video Art was an interactive installation that used Thomas DeFanti’s ZGRASS.

Giloth herself explains: “Using a joystick and buttons the user to could create a simple image and then using that image and its 7 simple symmetries create more complex drawings. Additional software and hardware designed by T. DeFanti and D. Harris. 10 plotter drawings were included in the exhibition. Hardware: Datamax Zgrass UV-1 machine with a custom interface.”

body: David Em transitioned from traditional painting to computer-generated art in the late ’70s. Experimenting with electronic manipulations of TV images, Em collaborated with computer graphics pioneers at Xerox Palo Alto Research Center (PARC). His pivotal moment came at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL), where, as an artist-in-residence, he adapted scientist James Blinn’s visualization software to craft his own unique computer art style. Em’s creations, influenced by the deep space environment, earned him the first-ever artist’s monograph on digital art. Renowned author Ray Bradbury praised Em for wielding technology as a tool, not a threat, marking a transformative period in the evolution of generative art.

body: Arranged by Peter Beyls, this was one of the earliest electronic music festivals. The festival had its second edition in 1981 after debuting the previous year. It would be a full decade later, in the late ’80s and early ’90s, that electronic music festivals as we know them began appearing. The festival featured experimental computer animation in addition to music. The musicians involved included John Appleton, Morton Subotnick, Donald Buchla, John Chowning, Jean-Claude Risset and others.

As part of the larger computer graphics conference, SIGGRAPH hosted the Computer Culture Art Show ’81 in Dallas, Texas, USA. Curated by Darcy Gerbarg, the show was incredibly varied, featuring “many forms, including sculpture, painting, printmaking, drawing, ceramics, photography and filmmaking.”

Yet, “the common ground upon which these artists stand, the thread which ties this show together, is the shared utilization of high technology,” said Gerbarg. Gerbarg exhibited artwork at the exhibition as well, including May I, a patterned work on ceramic tile.

The show featured artists such as Edward Zajec, Colette and Charles Bangert, Nelson Max, Stan Vanderbeek, Copper Giloth, Rebecca Allen, Lillian Schwartz, Ken Knowlton, David Em, Ruth Leavitt, Joan Truckenbrod and Jim Blinn.

body: One of the foremost computer artists of the time, Yoichiro Kawaguchi collaborated with the developers of the LINKS computer, which he also used to produce much of his work. His interest in organic, alien-like 3D forms was achieved algorithmically, mostly using a technology he called metaballs. An example of his randomly constructed, recursive algorithmic art is Tendril, also from 1981. In the book Digital Image, he refers to his work as digital art in one of the first instances of the term’s use. Another thing he has in common with Harold Cohen, yet for which Kawaguchi is significantly less credited, is the pioneering of AI art. His GROWTH model, which he began working on in the late ’70s is some of the first instances of evolutionary concepts in art. Further, his work more closely aligns with today’s machine learning—and AI art—than Cohen’s Expert System, logic based AI. 1981 also saw the beginning of his famous Growth Model going public as he would release a seminal paper 1982 on his findings. This paper would see him rise to international prominence.

body: Music Television (MTV), the first 24-hour television station based on music videos, was launched on 1 August 1981, a seminal day in the history of digital creativity and storytelling. MTV’s popularization of music videos fostered a culture of dynamic, short-form visual expression. This cultural shift towards innovative visuals and rapid editing techniques would influence all digital expression, including digital generative art. By popularizing unconventional visual aesthetics and embracing experimental techniques, MTV helped shaped the digital aesthetic of the ’80s and sparked a mindset receptive to the video as an art form.

body: This exhibition at MoMA highlighted pioneering collaborations between artists and technology in the 1970s. By showcasing innovative computer-generated video works, it helped establish video art. It highlighted the evolving relationship between art and emerging technologies, providing a platform for experimentation and creative exploration. Artists including Copper Giloth, Dan Sandin, Tom DeFanti and Jane Veeder showed algorithmic imagery and interactive work. The exhibition’s fusion of art and technology catalyzed a mindset that later artists embraced, leading to the exploration of code-based, evolving artworks characteristic of the digital generative art movement.

body: In a major advancement in AI and Machine Learning research, Paul Werbos proposed using backpropagation to train neural networks at the “System Modeling and Optimization” conference in New York. The method was initially introduced by Seppo Linnainmaa in 1970 for automatic differentiation in complex systems.

Werbos’s adaptation of this algorithm marked a significant advancement in neural network training, enabling the efficient adjustment of network weights by propagating errors backward through the layers.
Jürgen Schmidhuber describes it as “essentially an efficient way of implementing Leibniz’s chain rule for deep networks.”

Backprop's roots go back further, though, to control theory: Henry J. Kelley published a precursor in 1960 for computing optimal flight paths, followed by Arthur E. Bryson and Stuart Dreyfus. Werbos’s own 1974 thesis included a preliminary discussion of applying it to neural networks.
This breakthrough became foundational to modern deep learning, influencing the development of widely used AI frameworks like TensorFlow and PyTorch.

body: The Commodore 64, also known as the C64, was an 8-bit device that helped popularize the personal computer. It democratized home computing, bringing affordable and accessible technology to artists as well as hackers. With its impressive graphics and sound capabilities, it catalyzed the growth of the video game industry and software development. Like the Amiga and Apple’s devices, the Commodore 64 helped alter humanity’s relationship with machines and computers. Bringing them from military, government and corporate control to one’s home demystified machines that only a decade earlier were associated, particularly in the art world, with the military and a severely unpopular Vietnam War fought by the United States, the leader in computing technology. Little-known pockets of illegal software crackers would also use the C64 (and other 8-bit devices) throughout the decade of the ’80s (and beyond!), helping to spawn the Demoscene. So-called “cracktos” were crackers that removed the software’s copy protection and added personalized cracked intros. Hugely influential for its role in democratizing computing and invigorating the creation of computing, the Commodore 64 remains one of the most iconic computers ever built.

body: The Magic Hand of Chance Series (1982–85) was the legendary “Algorist’s” first foray into software work. It was inspired by the chance work of Dadaist Hans Arp.

Verostko wrote of the series: “My first effort with coded procedures attempted to use the operating system of the computer as the form generator. This would be a form of ‘computer automatism,’ miming the work of certain late Dada and early surrealist works.I had in mind especially how artists like Hans Arp had experimented with dropping torn shapes of paper on the floor to achieve a composition with ‘chance’” arrangements.”

body: This famous paper in the history of computer graphics outlines the breakthrough that was fractal rendering, which is still hugely important to this day. This seminal work explores the simulation of randomness in visual representation, leading to the creation of realistic natural phenomena such as clouds and landscapes. The paper laid the groundwork for rendering complex, organic structures through algorithmic techniques based on Mandelbrot’s fractals. By integrating stochastic processes into graphics, the paper revolutionized visual effects and paved the way for today’s sophisticated CGI techniques, deeply impacting film, gaming, design and, of course, digital generative art.

The book showcases how computers generate and manipulate images and how these have impacted various industries, such as art, design and engineering. It was around this time. body: Most computer graphics up to this point were hard-edged and linear with crisp RGB colors. It was difficult to produce images that appeared truly organic or naturally realistic. Bill Reeves, then at Lucasfilm and later at Pixar, was an early contributor to the solution of this problem by introducing particle systems in a foundational paper published in 1983, “Particle Systems: A Technique for Modeling a Class of Fuzzy Objects,” presented at SIGGRAPH ’83. This is an entirely generative process, as Wayne E. Carlson explains in his book, Computer Graphics and Computer Animation: A Retrospective Overview:

“Each particle in the system is born (or generated), undergoes some dynamic changes, and dies. Particles in the system are generated semi-randomly within the bounds of some initial object. This space is termed the generation shape of the fuzzy object. Each of the particle’s attributes is given an initial value that may be fixed or may be determined by a stochastic process.” The power of a particle system is that these “graphical primitives” can be used to create nearly anything from simple points and lines to complex organic and inorganic systems (grass, fire, etc.). Particle systems were famously used in the 1982 film Star Trek II: The Wrath of Khan for the famous “genesis effect.” [Carlson, 562]

cite.label: Wayne E. Carlson. Computer Graphics and Computer Animation: A Retrospective Overview. p. 238, 562. The Ohio State University Press.

body: David Lee Chaum, an American pioneering cryptographer, released his dissertation, “Computer Systems Established, Maintained, and Trusted by Mutually Suspicious Groups.” This paper is considered the first known proposal for a blockchain protocol. It even included the code to implement the system. Throughout the '80s, Chaum would pioneer privacy and digital currencies. His idea of “blind signatures” allowed a user to create an untraceable digital payment. While Chaum’s work laid the groundwork for anonymous transactions, his proposed systems still relied on a centralized authority, raising concerns about privacy and control. Satoshi Nakamoto would go on to solve these issues. Nakamoto’s innovation was the consensus mechanism called Proof of Work, which enabled a network of computers to validate transactions without the need for a central authority. This decentralized approach addressed the issues of control and trust present in Chaum’s earlier work.

body: After working on his GROWTH algorithm for several years at this point, Kawaguchi exhibits his first artistic expression from the algorithm with Growth.

This truly groundbreaking piece by Kawaguchi, who developed the animation using a supercomputer in Osaka, Japan, is some of the earliest evolutionary and artificial life art. Thus, it is some of the first proto-AI art, as we know AI art today.

This piece explains more about the computing power that the brilliant Kawaguchi took full advantage of: “Kawaguchi worked with Professor Koichi Omura at the University of Osaka when his lab developed LINKS-1, a computer graphic system for realistic renderings.

The machine was unprecedented for its processing power and, unlike supercomputers at the time, consisted of 34–62 regular-size processors connected in a networked system for faster calculations and the easy removal of deficient parts. From summer 1982 to spring 1983—an extraordinarily short duration process—Omura and Kawaguchi used LINKS to develop Growth: Mysterious Galaxy, a complex, 5-minute-long animation sequence that stunned the computer art community at ACM SIGGRAPH that year, including Pixar’s then-president Ed Catmull, who noted the piece’s unique sharpness and image quality.”

body: As Grant Taylor points out, the title of this essay by art critic Grace Glueck in the New York Times is both a nod to James Joyce “as well as a parallel to the first article that pushed computerized art into the realm of popular culture: John R. Pierce’s 1965 Playboy article entitled ‘Portrait of the Machine As a Young Artist.’” Taylor continues by quoting Glueck’s opening: “‘Given what we’ve seen of it to date, it’s small wonder that when we hear the term “computer art” our attention begins to wander. By now we’ve developed an understandable resistance to the boring optical shenanigans that result when computers are programmed to make drawings by technicians who lack the imagination of artists.’” The article’s broad panning of computer-programmed work provides a necessary temperature check on the state of technology and art. While computers themselves were finally becoming the beloved devices we know them as today, the art produced by them was still considered in a far less positive light.

body: German photographers Bernd and Hilla Becher have been instrumental in carrying on the twentieth-century Bauhaus tradition of the geometric aesthetic. Over the course of several decades, the couple photographed European and North American water towers. Their updated portrayal of the Bauhaus aesthetic was both a celebration of the rigidity of form but also commented on the idealistic promise of the Bauhaus with scenes of dilapidation. body: Developed by Apple, the Lisa was one of the first commercial personal computers with a GUI (Graphical User Interface). Lisa was short for “Local Integrated Software Architecture” as well as the name of Apple co-founder Steve Jobs’s daughter. Lisa holds crucial importance in the history of computer graphics as one of the first personal computers to feature a graphical user interface (GUI) and a mouse. It introduced intuitive visual elements like icons, windows and menus, setting the foundation for modern user interactions with computers. While commercially unsuccessful due in large part to its high price tag, the Lisa’s GUI concept profoundly influenced subsequent Apple products, notably the Macintosh. Its user-centric design revolutionized computer interaction by making it more accessible and user-friendly.

body: Rise of the demoscene

The demoscene began out of the software cracking community that developed in Europe around this time when legal protections were more nebulous. Legal protection for software arrived later in much of Europe, the United Kingdom legislating in 1985 and the European Community harmonizing in 1991. Legislation in Europe was enacted in the late '80s and throughout the ’90s. In the US, however, legislation was enacted in 1980, meaning that the demoscene and cracker/hacker scene would be more prevalent in Europe, where greater liberties could be taken with software (and those liberties became the expectation). As video games and the personal computer began to emerge in the late ’70s and early ’80s, crackers would remove the software copy protection from computer games on the Atari and Commodore 64. It became a challenge in the early ’80s for young video game enthusiasts to remove these copy protections to the point where a community began to form. The first to crack a new game would win prestige within the cracker community. Eventually, crackers took it a step further by changing the software of the game itself and adding their own personal intro to their copy, which they would share and distribute amongst friends at parties. While cracked screens began appearing as early as the Apple II, it wasn’t until the early ’80s that the practice became more mainstream. By the late ’80s and early ’90s, this practice of cracking and its community would evolve: “from people cracking games to writing graphic/sound demonstrations that showed off the computer they had just learned to program. Sure, cracking games was still popular, but some people decided that learning about the machine and using it as a tool for creativity was cooler” than cracking one dime-store game after another." -Demoscene activist Jim “Trixter” Leonard. This quote highlights the connection between the demoscene and digital generative art, as the demoscene carried on the tradition, since around this period in the early ’80s, of creativity in computer coding and creative expressions with software.

body: As mentioned as a key “under the radar” event in generative art history by Casey Reas in an interview with Le Random, the exhibition of Harold Cohen’s AARON at major institutions around the world was sadly an outlier in terms of computer-generated art’s institutional acceptance.

Reas continues: “We always talk about the fact that institutions have never supported generative art. And I think that they haven’t at all, in a really awful way, but there are exceptions. Harold Cohen had AARON making drawings at the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art (SFMOMA) and the Tate Gallery in London. Those are really big events that we should promote more. Harold was an extraordinary pioneer in the field.”

Cohen’s SFMOMA show was in 1979, and 1983 is when AARON appeared at Britain’s Tate Gallery, a critical moment of exposure to the legacy art world that was all too rare in computer-generated art’s history.

body: Artist Melvin Prueitt’s well-received publication explained how computers were being used at the time to create art. It also included a variety of computer-generated work. According to Grant Taylor in When the Machine Made Art, the book “reflected a newfound optimism in computer art.” [Taylor, 160] Taylor continues about Prueitt’s work: “The book follows many of the computer graphic publications of the period, which outline the different techniques and their application in science, business, and entertainment. Although Prueitt’s publication was concerned mostly with art, scientists and technologists produced much of the work, and the publication had a tendency to view the imagery through scientific paradigms and metaphors.” [Taylor, 160]

William Gibson’s classic novel reimagined the sci-fi genre. Optimistic visions of the future with their jetpacks and flying cars were replaced with a darker alternative, helping to popularize the cyberpunk aesthetic and its associations with the ’80s and ultimately the digital aesthetic. Dystopian societies dominated by mega-corporations and drugs served as the backdrop for hacker anti-heroes to resist. In addition to impacting the aesthetics of the 1980s that persist to this day, the book also captured the spirit of the anti-establishment hacker culture, which has been instrumental in forming crypto-art, separate from generative art.

body: Order Out of Chaos: Man’s New Dialogue with Nature by Ilya Prigogine and Isabelle Stengers first published in French in 1979, is a groundbreaking book that explores the concept of chaos theory and its relevance to various scientific disciplines. Prigogine, a Nobel laureate in chemistry, and Stengers, a philosopher, probe how chaos theory revolutionizes our understanding of complex systems and the natural world. In the context of digital generative art, this book helped to popularize the field of complexity and mythologize the role of the scientist, according to Grant Taylor in When the Machine Made Art. the idea that seemingly random and chaotic processes can lead to the emergence of order and beauty. Digital artists have long drawn inspiration from chaos theory to create artworks that reflect the balance of order and chaos in the world. Chaos theory, in particular, encouraged artists to experiment with algorithms and computational methods to generate patterns found in nature.

body: This seminal book, comprised of twenty-five essays, explores the evolving landscape of contemporary art in the post-modern era, marking a critical shift in art discourse by examining the rejection of modernist principles and the emergence of new artistic paradigms. The essays collected here discuss how artists began to embrace a more pluralistic approach, drawing from diverse traditions and mediums and challenging traditional hierarchies and categories. The book highlights elements of the postmodern framework that were here to stay, especially looking at work through a diverse set of lenses in careful context and the production of work through various media. This book is particularly significant for the development of digital art because it helped establish the intellectual framework for understanding art in the digital age. It laid the groundwork for appreciating digital art’s departure from traditional forms, highlighting the importance of interactivity, non-linearity and the fusion of art and technology, which reflect its roots in lumino-kinetic art and op art.

Another important postmodern text, published in French in 1979, this one was harshly critical of computers and particularly their use in art. The book argued that computers and society’s adaptation to them would have long-term negative consequences. Grant Taylor in When the Machine Made Art explains how Lyotard bleakly argued that the computerization of society would “reduce society to an efficient system, founded on the best possible input/output calculation.”

body: This series of works by Edward Zajec would continue until 1987.
Art historian Frank Popper explains the significance of Chromas, which Zajec references on his website:

“Edward Zajec sees his work not only in the narrow perspective of exploring the computer as an image generator, but also in the wider context of the expanded communication possibilities deriving from the interaction of art and technology. His ideas and techniques are concerned with the fluid articulation of colour and form in time.

The focus is not on the choreography of forms in motion (animation), but rather on those transitional states where dimensions interpenetrate, motifs dissolve into patterns and the geometric blends with the organic. Zajec aims beyond even this in trying to formulate some codes for a hypothetical language of light and sound (Orphics).

In a work called Chromas, crossed rays dissolve into one of several possible derivatives while modulating from a siena/cobalt to an ultramarine/green tonality. The actual unfolding of the images is based on the rhythms and sounds of a composition for piano by the contemporary Italian composer Giampaolo Coral.
Chromas is an attempt to develop and manipulate an aural theme in terms of colour and form. Thus the formative principle behind this development is not shape animation but thematic transformation.
-Frank Popper

body: One of the earliest German cracker groups, based in Dortmund, the German Cracking Service was among the groups whose crack intros anticipated the demoscene, especially on the C64. Legendary members of the group included 1103/JEDI and Snoopy. Their earliest catalogued intro, carrying the iconic three stripes, dates to 1984. You can still view their 1984 cracktro in a similar style, now introducing the game Slamball. The group’s activity was disrupted in the mid-1980s, though releases under the GCS name continued into 1988. Talented programmers, many members went on to have successful careers in early video games and software. These are some of the earliest whispers of the Demonscene.

body: Directed by Ridley Scott, this iconic commercial premiered during the Super Bowl, showcasing Apple’s Macintosh computer release. Its significance lies in its revolutionary approach to advertising, blending cinematic storytelling with technology. The ad presents a dystopian narrative inspired by George Orwell’s 1984, where a totalitarian regime is disrupted by a rebellious heroine wielding a sledgehammer. This commercial introduced the world to the concept of personal computing as a tool for liberation and creativity, emphasizing the Macintosh’s potential to empower individuals. In the context of digital generative art history, this commercial highlights the transformative power of computers, foreshadowing their role as the dominant creative tools of artists and designers around the world. The commercial also plays on the bad reputation that computers had due to their association with war and the military. This skepticism had remained around computers since as far back as the 1950s. These powerful, society-changing (and ending) machines that had been kept away from the general public for decades were finally becoming available as a commercially viable mass-market product. The world would genuinely never be the same.

body: From 1984 to 1988, Cubicomp specialized in computer-aided design (CAD) software and played a pivotal role in the development of 3D computer graphics on the personal computer. Cubicomp’s PictureMaker and ModelMaker software was instrumental in revolutionizing how artists and designers created and visualized complex 3D models. Additionally, Picture Maker was some of the earliest PC-based 3D animation software and was used by artists such as Victor Acevedo. He used the Cubicomp to create works including Wired Couple Series (1989-1990), 6.26.27.86 (1989-1991) and Tell Me the Truth (1989-1990), which entered the Victoria and Albert Museum in 2008 as part of the Patric Prince gift, the museum dating the print it holds to 1991. Acevedo spoke to Peter Bauman (Monk Antony) about Cubicomp, saying: “After my early experiments with algorithmic computer graphics in 1983 and 1984, in early 1985, I moved to the Cubicomp system because I could interactively and visually build polyhedral models, combine them with digitized photographs and animate image sequences. I wanted to expand on the type of hybrid geometrical imagery that I had developed with traditional analog media in the years 1977–1984.”

body: Founded by John Warnock and Charles Geschke, Adobe Systems in 1984 unveiled PostScript, a groundbreaking page description language and computer graphics technology that played a pivotal role in the history of digital art and graphic design, used by artists such as Mark Wilson. PostScript empowered artists, designers, and publishers to create high-quality, scalable graphics and text for both print and digital media. This innovation helped popularize digital typography and graphic design, as it provided a standardized language for describing page layouts and graphics, ensuring consistency across different output devices. The release of PostScript impacted the graphic arts industry by simplifying the printing process and enabling the creation of complex, vector-based artwork, as demonstrated, again, by Mark Wilson. It pushed us toward the desktop publishing revolution, which would give rise to ever more accessible and sophisticated design tools.

body: A critical technique in computer graphics, the distributed ray tracing algorithm, was developed by Loren Carptenter, Robert Cook and Thomas Porter for Lucasfilm and described in detail in this paper. Carpenter famously also developed fractal techniques for motion graphics in 1982. Distributed ray tracing allowed for motion blur effects.

Ray tracing enables the rendering of advanced lighting phenomena such as “shadows, reflections, and refracted light, phenomena that are difficult or impossible with other techniques.” However, there were limitations that Carpenter and his team solved, as outlined in the paper:

“By distributing the directions of the rays according to the analytic function they sample, ray tracing can incorporate fuzzy phenomena. This provides correct and easy solutions to some previously unsolved or partially solved problems, including motion blur, depth of field, penumbras, translucency, and fuzzy reflections.”

body: One of the most well-known and beloved PCs of all time, the Amiga’s introduction marked a significant leap in personal computing capabilities, particularly in graphics and multimedia performance. More critical to this story, it was instrumental in altering humanity’s relationship with machines. At the time, PCs like the Amiga were often derided as toys for “nerds,” yet now these early adopters appear visionary, seeing the potential of these humanity-shaping machines.

The device itself was equipped with advanced graphics and sound chips, enabling artists and designers to explore new creative interventions, as it quickly gained a devoted following among digital creatives.

The Amiga’s goal was to compete with Apple’s Macintosh and the IBM PC but with better sound and graphics. The Amiga, at $1,295 and cheaper than the Macintosh, was the only one of its competitors at the time that could run multiple programs at once. Additionally, according to this history:

“One of the key features of the Amiga was its custom graphics and sound chipset, which allowed it to display graphics and play sound that was far superior to what was possible on other personal computers. This made the Amiga a popular choice for artists and musicians, who used it to create animations, music, and other multimedia content.”

The Amiga’s capacity to handle sophisticated graphics and animations was foundational for the development of digital art and animation. It became a favored platform for pioneering digital artists, showcasing its potential at the intersection of technology and art. This platform’s influence on the emerging demoscene and computer art communities was profound, fostering experimentation with generative visuals and interactive experiences.

The launch of the Commodore Amiga in 1985 catalyzed the evolution of digital generative art by providing accessible, powerful tools for artists, contributing significantly to the medium’s growth and diversification in the years to come.

body: In this masterpiece of computer animation, Calculated Movements, Larry Cuba demonstrates his painstaking method of computer animation, creating elaborately choreographed scenes using basic elements that are repeated and arranged in a hierarchical fashion. As each level builds on the one before it, Gene Youngblood wrote that “if there is a Bach of abstract animation it is Larry Cuba,” creating aesthetically stunning compositions with intricate mathematical structures and cascading designs. Inspired by abstract animation pioneers such as Viking Eggeling and Oskar Fischinger, Cuba created Calculated Movements at his Santa Cruz studio with a Datamax UV-1 personal computer and Tom DeFanti’s ZGRASS graphics language. Cuba could now work with solid areas and volumes, breaking away from the conventional dot-based rendering thanks to this raster-graphics system.

body: In what may be the first creative coding book for artists, Mark Wilson published the seminal Drawing with Computers. The book served as manual for anyone to pick up and learn about making art with computers. In the mid-80s when the book was released, there was intrigue and enthusiasm for art by algorithms but it was difficult to learn. Wilson’s book filled this gap and would prove influential to artist and educator Travess Smalley, who spoke to Wilson about the book and much more in his profile on Le Random Editorials.
Also read this piece by Wilson himself on Le Random Editorials, where he reflects on his practice in his own words.

body: Originally published in 1971, this updated edition of the book reaffirmed its enduring relevance by including nearly fifteen more years of history. Franke’s work has been instrumental in introducing computer-generated art to a broader audience, and the re-release solidified his position as a pioneering figure in the field. The book highlights the history, methods and theoretical foundations of computer art as a movement, as only Franke could. Thus, the reissue not only served as a historical record of the early days of computer art but also underscored the ongoing evolution of the practice.

body: First developed in 1983 and formally described in 1995, Ken Perlin’s groundbreaking invention of Perlin Noise marked a watershed moment in the history of computer graphics and digital generative art that reverberates to this very day (just check out the latest release on fxhash). Perlin, a computer scientist and computer graphics pioneer, created this algorithm to generate naturalistic textures for Disney’s animated film "Tron.” Perlin Noise quickly became a foundational tool in computer graphics, offering a method for simulating intricate, organic patterns such as clouds, fire, and terrain. Its ability to create complex, visually appealing randomness with controllable characteristics transformed the artistic and technical possibilities of digital art and animation. Perlin noise played a vital role in shaping the aesthetic of digital landscapes, making it an essential tool for artists, game developers and filmmakers. Artist Emily Xie added this to the author, Peter Bauman, about Perlin: “Ken Perlin develops Perlin Noise, a gradient noise function that generates natural-appearing randomness. It was a huge stepping stone for graphical computing, allowing simulation of the natural world with realistic surfaces, patterns and textures. Perlin noise has been integral to generative art and is considered a foundational technique of the space.”

body: The Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) Media Lab opened its doors under the visionary leadership of Nicholas Negroponte and Jerome Wiesner. This event marked a significant turning point in the history of digital innovation, research, and generative art. The MIT Media Lab became a crucible of interdisciplinary collaboration, bringing together artists, engineers, designers, and scientists. Under Negroponte’s guidance, it fostered a creative environment where groundbreaking technologies and digital artistry could flourish. The lab’s pioneering work in fields such as computer graphics, virtual reality, and human-computer interaction influenced the development of digital art by providing access to cutting-edge tools and expertise. It served as a breeding ground for generative artists and researchers who explored the creative possibilities of emerging technologies. Nicholas Negroponte’s vision and the MIT Media Lab’s collaborative spirit have left an indelible mark on the digital art landscape. Their contributions have inspired generations of innovators and artists, shaping the ever-evolving intersection of technology and creativity.

body: Shoe-Field (1982–89), an interactive artwork begun with a performance in a Berkeley computer store, offered a unique exploration of personal feelings about footwear. Participants responded to shoe-related questions, resulting in a unique “shoe-psyche charge” represented by five plot patterns. The interactive aspect extended to choosing shoes from a chart, which influenced a podiatric Rorschach plot. Shoe-Field’s significance stands as a further example of experimentation combining technology and interactive personal expression, allowing participants to investigate the impact of individual choices on their perceived shoe psyche. The artwork exemplifies how creative expression and technology can combine in ways that are novel yet clearly carry on the lineage of the history of art and technology.

body: Computer scientist Craig Reynolds introduced the groundbreaking Boids algorithm, a significant milestone in the history of digital generative art and artificial life simulations.

Inspired by the mesmerizing patterns of bird flocking and fish schooling, Reynolds' Boids simulated the collective behavior of autonomous agents. It allowed these virtual creatures, or “boids,” to navigate their digital world by following a few simple rules: separation, alignment and cohesion. These rules gave rise to intricate and lifelike group dynamics in computer-generated animations and simulations.

Reynolds' work not only fascinated computer scientists and animators but also inspired a generation of artists, including Casey Reas, who mentioned this development to Le Random. Boids became a powerful metaphor for exploring the emergent complexity that arises from the interactions of simple entities.
Boids remains a symbol of the fruitful crossroads between technology, nature and artistic expression.

body: Langton’s ant was a cellular automaton created by Christopher Langton. Operating on a two-dimensional grid, this simple algorithmic system features an “ant” that follows a set of rules. Surprisingly, it produces emergent, complex, and beautiful patterns, blurring the line between randomness and determinism.

This phenomenon laid the groundwork for a new era of generative art, inspiring artists and programmers to explore the aesthetic potential of algorithms based on organic life. Langton’s Ant demonstrated that, with basic rules and repetition, intricate, visually captivating patterns could emerge organically.
Artist Casey Reas mentioned this development to Le Random as an example of an important moment to include on the Timeline.

body: This book explores the emerging world of fractals, the mathematical objects with intricate, self-replicating patterns coined by Benoit Mandelbrot but popularized in computer graphics by Loren Carpenter. Peitgen and Richter’s work played a pivotal role in introducing fractals to an even wider audience, emphasizing their aesthetic and artistic potential. The book’s vivid illustrations and accessible explanations captured the imagination of readers, bridging the gap between mathematics and art. It inspired a generation of artists, scientists and programmers to explore fractals as a creative medium.

body: This Ohio State University MA thesis, submitted by Richard Lucas, explored the aesthetics of computer art through a survey. Respondents to the survey included some of the field’s most respected voices, including Charles Csuri, Frank Dietrich, Hiroshi Kawano, Lillian Schwartz, Gene Youngblood and Frider Nake. The general findings were that traditional aesthetic criteria were largely deemed adequate for computer art evaluation.

body: The 1986 Biennale’s theme, Art and Science, was a topic largely ignored by major institutions for the past decade.
The event marked what Grant Taylor in When the Machine Made Art described as a renewed “interest in technoscience paradigms” of the time. It did but only to a point.

The event may have been indicative of a growing acceptance of science and technology in the arts after video games and personal computers helped dull techno-science fears of prior decades. Yet this resurgence in interest at the Biennale largely covered work in the firs thalf of the twentieth century as opposed to focusing on the most contemporary applications of science and art, such as the work of Craig Reynolds or Loren Carpenter.
Jasia Reichardt, beloved curator of Cybernetic Serendipity, covered “this special event with its unexpected juxtapositions of ideas and objects.” She continued, saying:

“The Art and Science exhibition was the major event of the Biennale. It covered Alchemy, Space, Biology, Technology and Informatics, Wunderkammer (Cabinet of Curiosities), Colour, and Science in the Service of Art.”

body: Edmonds moved from Leicester Polytechnic to Loughborough, establishing the Loughborough University of Technology Computer Human Interaction (LUTCHI) Research Centre. This would serve as his new base to continue exploring the intersection of art and technology. He would be joined by Stephen Scrivener, who made LUTCHI a pivotal research center investigating the amalgamation of computers, art and technology. The center had a particular focus on Human-Computer Interaction (HCI), becoming a thriving hub for artists and researchers, including luminaries like Stephen Bell. Notably, it played a crucial role in fostering the transition of individuals, such as Sean Clark, from computer scientists to artists. Clark and Edmonds continue to be active in the Computer Arts Society to this day. LUTCHI’s legacy can be felt decades later.

body: In the SIGGRAPH 1986 Art Show Catalogue, Ken Knowlton wrote an essay that captured the frustration within computer art that legitimacy had continued to elude the community, according to Grant Taylor in When the Machine Made Art.
Taylor describes the article as Knowlton asking a question yet the article is actually an explanation, Knowlton telling us, “Why It Isn’t Art Yet.” There is no question mark at the end of the title.
Knowlton felt that, despite more than twenty years making the art himself and considering himself a computer artist:

“We are not yet beyond the gee-whiz stage of cuteness, of stunts, and of novelty for its own sake. In order for the artist to get into serious art, he/she must have a more nearly complete command of the tools, including the understanding and ability to build, redefine and/or augment them.”

He concludes the essay by saying: “At this point, it does not make much sense to me to be trying to produce better computer art. The more appropriate challenge is to create better environments for the development of art-making tools.”
This call for better tooling would take time to be answered but would be steadily developed over the next fifteen years, culminating in Processing.

body: This groundbreaking book, The Blind Watchmaker, by Richard Dawkins ignited a paradigm shift in the discourse surrounding evolution and biology in art. According to Grant Taylor in When the Machine Made Art, this book’s importance cannot be overstated: “One of the most important shifts for computer art was the work of the evolutionary biologist Richard Dawkins.” Taylor explains that this is because of Dawkins’s use of simulated artificial organisms called “biomorphs” that Dawkins created “seeking to illustrate how complexity could be generated by simple rules.”

body: Woman of War (1986) and Lady of the Wild Things (1983) by Liliane Lijn stand as striking testaments to the intersection of art, feminism, performance and computers during this era. Lijn’s computer-controlled, kinetic sculptures made from steel and lasers confront societal norms and gender roles in all fields. Not what comes to mind for many when they think of “computer art,” Lijn’s sculptures feature the dynamism of light, kineticism and symbolism. The pieces challenge viewers to contemplate the complexities of womanhood and the wild, untamed spirit within, hinting that technology could serve as an empowering agent.

body: Rebecca Allen’s Modélisation d’un visage represents the artist’s continued work with computer-generated imagery of the human form and its movement. This work, which translates to “Modeling a Face” in English, encapsulates the essence of early digital art experimentation with 3D modeling techniques that were cutting-edge at the time.
Modélisation d’un visage besides being a technical achievement, also explores the complexities within real and digital representation, provoking contemplation about identity and perception.
More about Allen: Pioneer of generative motion

Inspired by the aesthetics of motion, Rebecca Allen’s decades-long career spans innovations in video, performance and installation art. Her work also examines themes such as gender, identity and technology’s impact on humanity.

Educated at both RISD and MIT, Allen feels comfortable in an artist studio as well as a research lab. Her scientific research informs her artistic practice, where she explores topics such as human motion simulation and artificial life algorithms.
Allen understood, early in her career, the power of the computer as an artistic tool. In Swimmer (1981), she created one of the first examples of computer animation capturing human motion.

In 1986, she collaborated with Kraftwerk on the revolutionary music video for “Musique Non-Stop.” It was one of the earliest examples of rendered 3D graphics in a music video. "My artistic goal was to define a digital aesthetic, and my research aim was to get the face to move, to express and to talk.”

Her interactive installation, Bush Soul (#1) in 1997 incorporated Allen’s research into artificial life and virtual environments. She created a generative space where participants could role-play as avatars in a virtual world.
Allen’s artistic vision and technical mastery led her to collaborate with other artists, including Nam June Paik, Peter Gabriel and John Paul Jones (Led Zeppelin).

Her work is also in the permanent collections at the Centre Pompidou, the Whitney Museum of American Art and MoMA. Allen recognized the impact of technology on human behavior, seeking generative techniques for art creation that explored this dynamic. She not only had the brilliance to invent new technologies, but she also had the creative vision to incorporate them into her artistic practice.

body: This small exhibition in Connecticut, where Mark Wilson is based, featured many of the prominent computer artists of the 1980s. The show defied was a relative rarity in that it showed work in North America in a fine art setting as opposed to being attached to technological and scientific conferences. The show demonstrated that art made by computers was still continuing to gain acceptance.

According to this review in the New York Times, while there was excitement for the event, many viewers found the results underwhelming, especially given the sophisticated tools involved. The exhibition featured works by various artists and mediums, including the early experiments by the legendary Darcy Gerbarg in computer-generated abstract art.

Mark Wilson and Manfred Mohr’s highly detailed computer-generated pieces came closest to fulfilling the expectations of the general public. Margot Lovejoy incorporated computer-derived images into three-dimensional constructions, addressing societal changes.

The exhibition also included computer-generated motion in videos set to music. Lillian Schwartz’s steel mobile, programmed to move uniquely for years, was exhibited and particularly appreciated at the event, according to the New York Times review. Visitors could interact with painting programs on Apple computers in a back room, offering a glimpse into the future of computer art.

body: In 1986, Steve Jobs, the visionary co-founder of Apple, made a historic move by purchasing Lucasfilm’s computer graphics division and incorporating it as Pixar. This acquisition, which initially seemed like an unconventional venture, would go on to reshape the computer graphics industry. Pixar, at the time, was a small computer graphics division of Lucasfilm, experimenting with computer-generated imagery. Under Jobs’s leadership, Pixar would evolve into an animation powerhouse, revolutionizing not only computer-generated images but filmmaking itself. In 1995, they released Toy Story, the world’s first feature-length computer-animated film, setting a new standard for animated storytelling using computers, a trend that to this day has not been reversed.

MediaLab/UnB fosters a dynamic synergy between art and technology while addressing the socio-artistic and political issues of contemporary society.

body: Lillian Schwartz’s Mona-Leo was the artist’s attempt to use computers to analyze portraits of both Leonardo da Vinci and the Mona Lisa. According to Schwartz, “With Unix-based machines, she proved indisputably that Leonardo used himself as the final model for the Mona Lisa.”
More about Schwartz: Pioneer of computer-generated film

Schwartz’s vision to innovate with the latest tools led to a career of genre-shattering experimentation. She had “an intense interest in new materials,” which would remain throughout her career. Mirroring computer art’s own genealogy, she worked in lumino-kinetic, “light box” sculptures before turning to computers.

Her kinetic work brought her in contact with the E.A.T. (Experiments in Art and Technology) group. This led to Schwartz’s “Proxima Centauri” being selected by MoMA for its epochal “The Machine as Seen at the End of the Mechanical Age” (New York) in 1968.

She then joined Bell Labs as its first female artist, working on her own and with the likes of Ken Knowlton. Here, she would create some of the lab’s most important early work with computers. At Bell Labs, she experimented with computer-generated film, combining traditional techniques with the latest digital methods. Her films were at once modernist and based on abstract geometric forms, yet they generated a vast array of advanced computer imagery.

Schwartz’s pioneering use of various physical and digital media pushed the limitations of technology to embrace the unexpected. Her career showed how, in her own words, "computers can be made to accommodate the entire breadth of artistic thought.”
The work was featured in Frank Popper’s Art of the Electronic Age.

body: In 1987, Apple Inc. introduced the revolutionary HyperCard software, forever altering personal computing. Created by Bill Atkinson, HyperCard was a groundbreaking hypermedia system that enabled users to create interactive “stacks” of digital cards containing text, graphics and multimedia elements, akin to today’s hypertext and precursor to the World Wide Web.

According to Casey Reas, this software was significant for the development of generative art. As he told Le Random, “HyperCard software was really essential. A lot of poets and a lot of artists were making Hypercard stacks in this multimedia environment to make generative work with.”

HyperCard’s intuitive “stack” structure, combined with a user-friendly interface, empowered individuals, educators and artists to craft interactive content without extensive programming knowledge. It was a pioneering tool for multimedia authoring, paving the way for interactive presentations, educational materials and early digital art, all before the emergence of the World Wide Web in a few short years.

HyperCard also influenced the early web’s aesthetics. According to Thomas Dreher, “Pei-Yuan Wei was inspired by HyperCard when he developed the browser "Viola WWW,” one of the earliest web browsers in the early-90s.

body: MacroMind Director 1.0 made its debut, forever transforming multimedia content creation. Developed by MacroMind, this pioneering software, later passing to Macromedia and then Adobe, allowed designers to craft interactive multimedia presentations and animations with remarkable ease relative to previous software.
A standout artist in the use of Director is LIA, who in the ’90s was at the forefront of this powerful language. She described in a conversation with Le Random:

“I got a copy of the program. I got the handbook, and I basically copied the Macromedia Director Handbook by hand twice until I understood what a function was. It was called a handler, and the language was lingo, and it still is or was, actually.
It was one of the most powerful programs ever out there. Macromedia Director.
It allowed people really quickly do some animations by dragging and dropping without knowing how to code, and then you could enter the next level by actually writing code.”
According to Casey Reas, this software was significant for the development of generative because, lerandom.art:
“When I was cutting my teeth in this world, everything was being made with Macromedia Director.

It preceded Flash as the medium that people were making work in. A timeline that I could get really excited about would be the tools that generative artists use and how that evolved over time. This time period was also the CD-ROM era. There were a number of extraordinary, experimental releases on CD-ROM made with Director, for example by LIA, which is also skipped over a lot.” LIA made her seminal 1999 net.art work Re-move with Macromedia Director.

What exactly made Director so successful? It can be partly explained by its revolutionary “score” metaphor, which simplified complex multimedia sequencing, enabling users to orchestrate audio, video and graphics with much greater ease than ever before. This innovation spurred the creation of interactive CD-ROMs, kiosks, and early web content.

As multimedia rapidly evolved, Director remained at the forefront, allowing creators to push digital storytelling forward. Its influence extended beyond creative coding and digital generative art to include educational software, immersive video games and filmmaking.

body: CompuServe introduced the Graphics Interchange Format, commonly known as the GIF, in 1987, which forever changed how we share and communicate through images on the internet. Developed by Steve Wilhite, the GIF was initially designed to efficiently store and transmit color images for CompuServe’s file downloading areas. Its innovative compression algorithm allowed for compact files that could be easily shared. This ease of sharing gained the attention of early Internet platforms. With the emergence of the Internet, the GIF quickly gained popularity due to its versatility and support for animations. It would play an instrumental role in the development of humor and meme culture online, a direct antecedent to net and eventually “crypto and NFT” art. The GIF’s looping graphics became a hallmark of early web culture and, two decades later, early NFT culture.

Goodman’s observation that fine artists were embracing computers with great enthusiasm signaled a departure from previous years' disinterest and outright hostility. This renewed optimism in the 1980s reflected a growing acceptance of digital art, in contrast to a more pessimistic ’70s. body: Thomas and John Knoll began their journey to revolutionize digital image editing with the development of Photoshop. Originally conceived as a way to showcase grayscale images on a monochrome display, this software would go on to redefine the creative possibilities of visual art and photography. Adobe licensed the software two years later, in 1989, and subsequent versions of Photoshop continued to innovate. The introduction of features such as layers, filters and an easy-to-use interface changed the way professionals and beginners approached image editing. Photoshop democratized image manipulation by enabling anyone with a computer to become a digital artist or photo editor. This is in stark contrast to the additional levels of difficulty previously required in terms of specialized coding knowledge, which could take years or decades to master. Since its inception, Photoshop has become an essential tool across diverse industries, from graphic design and advertising to photography and web design. Its name has become synonymous with image editing, and its impact on visual culture is immeasurable.

body: As an artist and research fellow at the IBM UK Scientific Centre, William Latham would first meet Stephen Todd, beginning a life-long collaboration that continues to this day. Their collaboration had foundations in artificial life and would profoundly impact evolutionary art, in many ways the basis for AI art as we know it today. While at IBM with Todd, they developed Mutator and FormGrow on IBM state of the art mainframe computers. Latham and Todd began working on the evolutionary art system Mutator at IBM in 1987. Lance Putnam and Peter Todd joined the Mutator work much later, on Mutator VR from 2016. Their work displayed “strange organic, often serpentine, forms, produced using [an] “alternative evolutionary software system” (developed with Stephen Todd and team), which William uses to pick and breed 3D forms freed from the limits of the human imagination.” According to Latham’s biography, “William’s work is focussed on using evolutionary processes to create art centered on the idea of 'Artist as Gardener,' an idea which originated from his time as Henry Moore Scholar at the Royal College of Art in the early eighties where he created his FormSynth drawings and etchings which were to become a blueprint for his later Mutator work.” The advancement of evolutionary art has had a profound and lasting impact on the generative art of today, as it helped spur the concept of generative art with changeable characteristics, particularly those that could evolve over time. This has specifically impacted AI art. The evolutionary work of Latham and Todd can be considered proto-machine learning art, as the evolving, breeding features of the program—drawn directly from cybernetics and its feedback loops—are the predecessors of machines processing data to perform instructionless tasks, modern machine learning. Prior to 1987, Latham developed his well-known Form Synth algorithm (1979-1986). Latham would continue at IBM until 1993. In particular, the work of Latham and Todd has influenced contemporary work in artificial life, including by Ciphrd and Sage Jenson.

body: Developed in 1986 but first shipped in 1987, Adobe Illustrator emerged as a groundbreaking vector graphics software, revolutionizing the design industry. Developed by Adobe Systems for the Apple Macintoush, Illustrator provided designers with a powerful toolset for creating scalable and precise, visually compelling illustrations. Its intuitive interface and robust features quickly made it an essential piece of software for graphic designers, allowing for the creation of logos, icons and intricate artwork. Illustrator is the companion product to Photoshop that focuses on areas of typesetting and logography in design. The program was a step forward in graphic design from software such as MacDraw and was the commercialization of Adobe’s PostScript.

body: With the introduction of the Mac II, Apple ushered in a new era of computing with the first 32-bit Mac. This desktop computer boasted groundbreaking features such as color graphics, expansion slots and enhanced processing power, making it the first Mac with color capabilities.

The Mac II became a powerhouse for creative professionals, offering unprecedented capabilities for graphic design, desktop publishing and multimedia production. For instance, with the right graphics card, the Mac II could handle up to 16.7 million colors. Its modular design and color capabilities transformed the Macintosh into a versatile platform, solidifying Apple’s impact on the PC market.
The machine was still quite expensive, selling at $3,898 for the most basic model, roughly $10,556 in 2023.

body: A transformative development occurred in the realm of personal computing with the availability of scanners for PCs. The newfound ability to convert photographs, artwork, and printed material into digital formats revolutionized content creation, graphic design, and document management. The integration of scanners into personal computing marked a significant step toward the digitization of visual information, paving the way for diverse applications across industries and contributing to the democratization of image digitization.

body: Verostko’s paper is said to have “identified biological analogues to autonomous form generating procedures. His ‘epigenetic art’ includes a limited edition of George Boole’s ‘Derivation of the laws illustrated with his own ‘personal expert system,’” known as Hodos.

Presented at FISEA in 1988 and published in Leonardo in 1990, the paper anticipated prompt-based AI in many ways, outlining a new era in art-making systems. Artists use program feedback to iteratively develop software, akin to refining compilers. The evolving software becomes a distinct art form, comparable to genetic code. Verostko envisions hybridization, coding art ideas from different creators, resulting in unique combinations like “Kandinsky-Mussorgsky” with audio and visual drivers. Anticipating future advancements, he sees artists easily constructing personal expert systems, fostering generational growth in improvisational works. In this uncanny process, software takes on a life of its own, requiring artists to humanize it—providing form and structure to align with artistic and life quality.

body: 1988 saw the inception of the ISEA conference, initiated by Theo Hesper and Wim van der Plas in 1986, which materialized as the “FIRST International Symposium on Electronic Art” (FISEA) in 1988. Conceived to establish a network exploring the intersection of art and science, the inaugural symposium unfolded in Utrecht, with satellite activities in Groningen and The Hague. ISEA from this point forward became a crucial platform for digital artists. Subsequent events spanned global locations, including Sydney, Minneapolis and Helsinki. Over time, ISEA evolved into a nomadic event, a distinctive feature shaping its history. The name was coined at FISEA in 1988 and the Inter-Society founded in 1990, laying the foundation for an enduring international platform fostering interdisciplinary discourse and the advancement of electronic art. The symposium’s impact on the development of the digital art from the late ’80s onwards is little-known but huge. Is fusion of academic discourse with creative showcases, facilitated interdisciplinary collaboration and showcased cutting-edge electronic art and technological innovations on a global scale for over three decades.

body: This moment serves as an additional example of digital machines entering people’s homes and altering the human-machine relationship and sentiment. In a watershed moment for digital mass media, FAX machines became widely available, altering the communication landscape. This technology breakthrough gave enterprises and individuals alike the power of fast document transmission. The FAX machine was a precursor to the instant document transfer we have now, altering how we shared ideas and interacted. As FAX machines spread, they cross geographical gaps, speeding up information flow. The machine and its wide-spread availability thus represent a watershed moment in the democratization of communication tools, signaling an era in which document transmission transcends physical constraints, opening up new avenues for global connectedness and collaboration.

body: One of the key moments in mass-media art but also in human history, Berners-Lee’s invention revolutionized the digital landscape as the visionary computer scientist conceived of the concept of the World Wide Web (WWW). The invention was also critical to the eventual development of NFTs. Working at CERN, he proposed a decentralized system to share and retrieve information, laying the foundation for the Internet we know today. By the end of 1990 he had built the first browser, server and web page, ushering in a new era of global communication. Berners-Lee’s invention broke down technological barriers, democratizing access to information. The rise of mass-media technology and art were critical steps in enabling NFTs. Thus, this can be seen as a critical step in the development of digital art, such as net art. Also, more broadly speaking, it’s a major step towards the global, collaborative and instantly shareable art environment we enjoy today.

body: The SIGGRAPH ‘89 conference marked a watershed point in computer art history. A significant panel session evolved among the convergence of creative minds, provocatively titled “Computer Art—An Oxymoron?” This debate, dubbed “Views from the Mainstream,” probed into the heart of artists' discontent and, according to Grant Taylor in When the Machine Made Art, was the first major attempt to critically study computer art. As the SIGGRAPH '89 debates progressed, philosophically divergent viewpoints emerged, providing the framework for a series of major journal publications. This historic event not only addressed the changing world of computer art, but it also sparked a critical perspective that would define the debate surrounding this dynamic junction of technology and creativity. The investigation also stands in contrast to contemporary belief that criticism in computer art has little precedence. The art show itself featured work from Ana Ursyn, Mark Wilson, Jean-Pierre Hebert, Hans Dehlinger, Brian Reffin Smith, Colette Bangert, Charles Bangert and Manfred Mohr.

body: Several instances around this time period signaled the end of “Computer Art” and the rise of “Digital” or New Media Art, as argued originally by Grant Taylor in When the Machine Made Art. The first instance was the art critic David Carrier, writing in Leonardo, rejecting computer art and casting a contemplative shadow on the movement by declaring, “it is genuinely unclear to me whether any art using computers is truly significant.” This was a watershed moment in our story, as computer art now grappled with an existential crisis.

Perhaps feeling the pressure of decades of lack of recognition, the remark alluded to the skepticism surrounding technology’s transformative power in art, ushering in an era of critical examination. Carrier would also not be the only one to give up on computer art over the years. The remark signals the crisis evident in a movement where it was a point of pride and distinction to make computer graphics from code. But as this was increasingly becoming possible with the use of design software, “computer art” as a unified movement was called into question. This year can be, in some ways, thought of as the end of “computer art,” as it had been known since the 1960s.
Taylor explains in further detail:

“The term ‘computer art’ had a fundamental problem which arose when there was a complex intertwining of traditional analog, electronic, and digital technologies, and when the artist had no desire to proclaim the medium as central to the work. In fact, artist Judson Rosebush proclaimed in 1989 that ‘computer art has become a meaningless term.’ That same year, Brian Reffin Smith proclaimed this to his readers: ‘Let us make an art that does not need the computer to justify it.’
Richard Wright in the 1989 SIGGRAPH Computer Art show catalogue also asks, “Does ‘Computer Art’ Still Exist?”

body: In an honest but heartbreaking article, Brian Reffin Smith’s philippic against computer art presented a devastating case against the entire movement that Smith helped pioneer. The text criticizes the state of computer art, arguing that it is often outdated, commercially driven and lacking true artistic significance. Smith points out that much of what is labeled as “computer art” is actually graphic design created for non-artistic purposes. The text highlights a disconnect between the computer art world and traditional art institutions, with galleries and critics often dismissing it. The author acknowledges some improvement in computer art but contends that it remains isolated from contemporary art problems and lacks genuine innovation. Calling for a more honest evaluation of computer art, the text also demands a focus on teaching the importance of ideas over technical aspects, and a shift towards creating computer art that challenges conventions and incorporates critical discourse. Smith encourages artists to explore the interactive capabilities of computers and produce work that transcends the need for technological justification. The conclusion emphasizes the need for courage and innovative ideas to truly advance computer art beyond its current limitations.

img.cap: Brian Reffin Smith's Text Text Piece, hung in the SIGGRAPH '89 art show: two columns of dense typescript flanking a band of orange and yellow marks, headed by a line of blocky computer lettering. It is a work by the author of 'Beyond Computer Art', not the essay.
img.credit: Brian Reffin Smith, Text Text Piece, 1988. Ink on paper, 8.25 x 11.75 in. Shown in the SIGGRAPH 1989 Art Show. ACM SIGGRAPH History Archives.

body: Digital creativity witnessed a revolution with the invention of Kid Pix. Developed by Craig Hickman and published by Broderbund Software in 1991, Kid Pix marked a paradigm shift in computer software designed for children. lerandom.art:

“Kid Pix is a drawing program written for children. It was made as a direct response to MacPaint (1984). And it includes a lot of generative drawing tools. You can drag your mouse across the screen and things drip down or you drag your mouse across the screen and all of these concentric circles emerge from that point.”

lerandom.art “I think the huge disappointment in Mac Paint, it’s an extraordinary piece of software but all it, is that it emulates existing tools. This is the airbrush tool. This is the Eraser tool. This is the Pen tool. Kid Pix branches out from there and makes drawing tools that are unique, and that can only be made with code. It really encouraged a generation of children to play with drawing in software.”

img.credit: Miki Yoshihito. Flickr. “SAKURAKO play KID-PIX.” 2011. flickr.com

body: Carnival, an exquisite work from Verostko’s Pathway Series, represents a five-decade exploration of unseen worlds. Verostko pioneers the convergence of software form-generators and fine-arts practice, rooted in the legacy of early twentieth-century abstraction. He creates visual worlds by combining computational precision with artistic contemplation using BASIC and DM/PL, Houston Instrument’s Digital Microprocessor Plotting Language. A “fine art form generator,” as Verostko referred to his algorithms, serves as a biological genotype in his methodology, encoding the information for form generation. Verostko’s works, created with a multipen plotter, reveal a meticulous dance of thousands of lines, with each pen change and occasional brush stroke orchestrated by software. As Verostko’s art transcends intentional representation, titles are arbitrary, reminiscent of labeling flowers. Instead, he intends for each piece to unfold as a unique journey into uncharted territories. These visual manifestations honor the dynamic processes that underpin their creation, inviting viewers to savor the mystery of coded procedures that result in unexpected grace and beauty.

img.credit: Roman Verostko, Carnival, Pathway Series, 1989. Ink on paper, 36 x 24 in. ACM SIGGRAPH History Archives.

body: In Postmodern Currents: Art and Artists in the Age of Electronic Media, Margot Lovejoy explores how art has changed with the rise of electronic media. Lovejoy takes a straightforward approach to dissecting the impact of technology on artistic expression in the postmodern era. The book studies how artists navigate traditional forms in the face of emerging technologies. Lovejoy’s work serves as a foundational text in the genealogy of electronic art.

body: Apple launched the Macintosh (Mac) Portable, ushering in a new era of portable computing. Weighing around 16 pounds, this ground-breaking device became the first battery-powered Macintosh, providing users with previously unheard-of mobility. The Mac Portable catered to professionals on the go, with a crisp active matrix display, a built-in trackball and the power of a desktop Mac. Despite its weight, this early attempt at a portable Mac was a major advancement in mobile computing technology. The Mac Portable paved the way for Apple’s portable product line to evolve, paving the way for the more compact and lightweight laptops that would follow, as well as the iPhone and iPad.

body: The Legible City, a game-changing interactive art installation, made its debut in Nagoya, Japan. The hardware and software were meticulously crafted by a dedicated team after being conceptualized by Jeffrey Shaw and Dirk Groeneveld. Cyclists rode stationary bikes through a virtual city made of computer-generated letters, which replaced actual architecture. The handlebars and pedals gave users control, fusing physical and virtual effort. The Manhattan version added color-coded fictional narratives for exploration. Legible City, which was shown at Artec '89 in Nagoya, SIGGRAPH '89 in Boston and Ars Electronica '89 in Linz, and later at MultiMediale 2 in Karlsruhe in 1991, remains a landmark in digital generative art, combining physical engagement with immersive, text-based cityscapes.

body: The introduction of Intel’s 80860 microprocessor marked a paradigm shift in processing power, with capabilities comparable to the formidable Cray 1 supercomputer. This microprocessor represented a significant advancement in computational efficiency and performance. The integration of Cray-level power into a single chip changed the computing landscape, opening up new possibilities for a wide range of applications, including in the visual arts.
